titre: Swimming Is Not a Natural Gesture
accroche: Marcel Mauss saw his own swimming technique become obsolete within a generation, and drew a theory of the body from it.
contenu_vulgarise:
Walking, swimming, carrying a child on the hip, or digging with a spade: we take these gestures to be self-evident, almost biological. The body, we assume, does what it has to do, regardless of culture. It is this self-evidence that the sociologist Marcel Mauss dismantles on May 17, 1934, in a lecture given before the Société de Psychologie (Society of Psychology) and published two years later in the *Journal de Psychologie* under the title “Les techniques du corps” (“Techniques of the Body”).

## The body as a social fact

Mauss calls “techniques of the body” the ways, specific to each society and transmitted as know-how, in which humans use their bodies (walking, swimming, running, sleeping, giving birth). None of this, he shows, is purely physiological: every gesture is learned, often without our being aware of it, by imitation of a model transmitted through education. A French swimmer of the 1930s does not swim like a Polynesian swimmer, nor like the swimmer he would have been a generation earlier.

Mauss illustrates the idea with his own experience: the swimming techniques he learned as a child, in the late 19th century, had already disappeared in his lifetime. “Our generation, here, has witnessed a complete change of technique,” he writes: the various kinds of crawl have replaced “the breaststroke with the head out of the water,” and the habit of swallowing water and then spitting it out has been lost. Swimmers of his day “considered themselves a sort of steamboat.” What the body “knows how to do” is therefore not fixed once and for all by biology: it is taught, forgotten, replaced, within a single lifetime, without any physical evolution having had time to play a part.

## What this shifts

Mauss's contribution goes beyond the case of swimming. He designates the body as an object in its own right for sociology. Neither only biological nor only psychological, it is shaped by what he calls “physio-psycho-sociological” assemblages: three inseparable dimensions in the slightest gesture. Before him, the body belonged almost exclusively to the natural sciences; after “Techniques of the Body,” it becomes a legitimate field of inquiry for anthropology.

The most useful shift, even today, comes down to a simple question to ask about any gesture you believe is spontaneous (running, sitting, carrying a weight, breathing during exertion): are you sure that no one ever showed it to you? The answer, most of the time, is no. And that is precisely what Mauss calls a technique of the body.

repere.texte: The lecture was given on May 17, 1934, before the Société de Psychologie and published in 1936 in the Journal de Psychologie: Mauss himself dates there, within his own lifetime, the disappearance of the swimming techniques he had learned as a child.
repere.source: Marcel Mauss, Les techniques du corps, Journal de Psychologie, vol. 32, 1936

carte.punch: Your way of swimming has an expiration date.
carte.idee: Marcel Mauss saw, within his own lifetime, the swimming technique he had learned as a child become obsolete. From this he drew a theory: walking, swimming, or carrying a child are learned gestures, not biological reflexes.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Marcel Mauss's Techniques of the Body: Why We Don't All Walk the Same Way

quiz.question: What does Mauss mean by “techniques of the body”?
choix: Learned and transmitted gestures, not purely biological reflexes
Religious rituals tied to bodily purification
Postures imposed by universal human anatomy
quiz.explication: For Mauss, walking, swimming, or carrying a child are skills transmitted by imitation within a given society, not reflexes fixed by human biology, hence their variation from one culture and one generation to the next.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When and where does Mauss first present “Techniques of the Body”?
choix: In 1936, in an article published directly in the Journal de Psychologie with no prior lecture
In 1897, as a continuation of Durkheim's work on suicide
On May 17, 1934, in a lecture before the Société de Psychologie
In the late 19th century, when he himself learns to swim
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Mauss presents his concept on May 17, 1934, in a lecture given before the Société de Psychologie, before the text was published two years later, in 1936, in the Journal de Psychologie.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly does Mauss say about the change in swimming technique that he himself experienced?
choix: That the various kinds of crawl replaced the breaststroke with the head out of the water
That this change comes from a gradual physical evolution over several generations
That swimming has remained fundamentally the same since his childhood
That only professional swimmers changed technique, not the general public
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Mauss writes that his generation witnessed a complete change of technique: the various kinds of crawl replaced the breaststroke with the head out of the water, and the habit of swallowing water and then spitting it out was lost.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Mauss mean by “physio-psycho-sociological” assemblages?
choix: A medical protocol used to study swimming
A classification of societies by their technical level
The name given to his method of fieldwork
Three inseparable dimensions, biological, psychological, and social, in the slightest gesture
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Mauss means that no gesture, even the most trivial, is purely biological: each inseparably combines a physiological, psychological, and social dimension, which makes the body a legitimate object for anthropology.
